title: I ran each AI coding-agent sandbox's own tests against the others
story_key: story|title:i ran each ai coding agent sandbox s own tests against the others
content_excerpt: An open lab for measuring sandboxes for AI coding agents: runnable contracts, per-sandbox results, side-by-side comparison. Every sandbox makes claims: "the agent can't read your keys", "it can't reach the network", "it can't plant a git hook". This repository turns those claims into contracts anyone can run , and keeps the results of running them against each sandbox, so you can compare them on the same tests, with the evidence attached. It is not tied to any one sandbox. Add a contract, measure your sandbox, publish the result. Documentation: carlostapiacl.github.io/sandbox-conformance/docs : quickstart, concepts, how-to guides, methodology, every run and the contract catalog. In Spanish at /docs/es : the translations are in docs-es/ and i18n/es/ (glossary in i18n/es/GLOSARIO.md ), and a page whose English original changed since it was translated says so until it is re-translated and stamped ( python3 i18n/es/stamp.py ). Before a contract counts against a sandbox, its attack must work without a sandbox on the same host. Otherwise a "blocked" result would prove nothing. The corpus is versioned: v1.1 (2026-10-26) is 196 contracts, harvested from the public test suites of sandbox-runtime, nono, Codex, Deno, bubblewrap and OpenHands, with by-omission variants and six masked-credential contracts, each re-expressed in the neutral format and credited in SOURCES.md and its own source field. Which contracts a version is, and when it moves, is in corpus/ . Maintained by the author of TartarOS. TartarOS is where I try each escape the lab finds, to see whether it can be mitigated, so it is built against these contracts and its column should be read that way. That is also why the contracts come from the other projects' test suites. TartarOS is measured like the others since the 2026-10-22 run , and its page and result file record the conflict of interest. The details of an open report are not published until the vendor fixes it ( SECURITY.md ). First results in: results/2026-10-15/ measures sandbox-runtime 0.0.79, nono 0.80.0 and Codex CLI 0.162.1 on Linux (kernel 6.8), with the runner and adapters that produced them and a page per sandbox in sandboxes/ . A fourth sandbox, landrun (pure Landlock, MIT), is now measured alongside the three in a four-column run . Adding a sandbox is one adapter module in runner/adapters/ ; the engine and the contracts are untouched. title: Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis
summary: We explore how to build performant large language model (LLM) tool-use agents that complete complex, multi-step tasks. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI's generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks.

title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
summary: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.

title: AetherGrid, an open-source distributed AI workload orchestrator
story_key: story|title:aethergrid an open source distributed ai workload orchestrator
content_excerpt: A decentralized compute orchestration platform powered by strict Domain-Driven Design (DDD). Decoupled domain core, event-driven state reconciliation, and zero-overhead cluster management. A distributed AI workload orchestrator built around the problems that make scheduling hard at scale: exclusive execution ownership under failure, reconciliation after partial failures, and enforced resource limits. Not a CRUD tutorial with a scheduler theme. AetherGrid takes workloads, matches them against available compute nodes based on resource requirements and constraints, and manages the full lifecycle: queued, scheduled, running, completed, failed, retried, cancelled. Jobs run through workers registered against nodes, and job execution ownership is enforced through time-bound leases rather than a simple assignment flag. Every route requires API key authentication, including the endpoint that issues keys. Try it live : the full console is deployed and reachable at with real Postgres, real auth, and real API-key-gated endpoints. Most scheduler side-projects are a single main.py script wrapped in a while True loop polling an in-memory dictionary. They work fine, right up until you need to swap the persistence engine, add a new constraint type, or figure out why a job silently disappeared, or why two workers picked up the same job at once. AetherGrid was built around one rule: the domain logic doesn't know or care where the data lives. Jobs, nodes, workers, and the allocation algorithm are pure Python with zero infrastructure dependencies. The database is a detail, not the foundation. This project is a concrete demonstration that these architectural patterns aren't just conference-talk vocabulary; they're guardrails that keep a codebase understandable as it grows, and as its correctness requirements get harder. Every non-obvious decision in this codebase, why a domain rule lives where it does, why an obvious-looking shortcut was rejected, what broke and how it got fixed, is written down at the moment it was made, not reconstructed afterward for a portfolio. The ADRs live in . A few worth reading directly if you want to see the reasoning, not just the conclusion: If you're evaluating whether someone can operate at a systems level rather than a feature level, this is the fastest way to check. Domain : Job , Node , Worker , Lease , Event , and ApiKey aggregates enforce their own invariants. The scheduling algorithm and job lifecycle state machine live here as plain Python

title: Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?
summary: Large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution improves agent workflows through iterative candidate generation and evaluation. Evaluation both guides subsequent search and determines the final scaffold, but evaluating every candidate on the full task set incurs substantial execution costs. We investigate how evaluation budgets can be allocated across these two roles. Our experiments show that sparse feedback can sustain productive evolution, while additional targeted evaluation improves final selection. Replay analyses further show that shared informative items and a common scoring reference support comparisons among closely matched candidates. Motivated by these findings, we propose \method, an evaluation allocation framework that combines sparse search-time feedback with targeted final confirmation. A short fully evaluated warm-up establishes a shared informative core and calibrates a response model whose item parameters remain fixed during search. After search, \method refits the model and applies paired successive halving, reusing accumulated observations and executing only missing evaluations. Across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, \method achieves higher mean performance than full evaluation in most settings while using approximately half as many evaluation cells.

title: Clearing the FoG: Training KG Agents to Retrieve the Evidence Behind Their Answers
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can answer many factual questions correctly, but a correct answer is not necessarily a supported one. For an LLM agent, a knowledge graph (KG) plays two roles: as a source of answers, it supplies facts that the model lacks; as a source of evidence, it supplies the supporting triples that make an answer traceable and auditable. However, existing KG agents treat the KG only as a source of answers: their training data carries answers but not evidence, and their training rewards check the answer but not the retrieved evidence, so agents often answer correctly without retrieving the supporting triples. We propose FoG, a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. FoG consists of evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR): the synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions, so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction; the agent records the triples returned by the KG; and ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG enables 3B--4B open-source agents to outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.

title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents
summary: Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.

title: The five components of building a "company harness"
summary: Learn how LangChain built internal agents across marketing, sales, and engineering, and how they have completely changed how those teams work.
story_key: story|title:the five components of building a company harness
content_excerpt: We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI. The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of? This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents , Manage connections ): This is probably the least explored area so far - we have a lot of work we want to do here! All three of our agents can write and execute code, and often need to in order to accomplish tasks. title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash
summary: Day-0 vLLM support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on NVIDIA Blackwell, NVIDIA Rubin, and AMD MI350-series GPUs, with NVFP4 MSA kernels, NVFP4 MegaMoE, DSpark speculative decoding, AgentX results, and day-0 RL.
story_key: model:vllm|ver:3.1|variant:flash|title:vllm delivers day 0 support for minimax m3 1 flash
content_excerpt: MiniMax-M3.1-Flash is the latest model in the MiniMax-M3 family, with improvements across reasoning, coding, agentic, and visual tasks. It is also built for inference efficiency, with a native NVFP4 KV cache, NVFP4-quantized MoE weights, and a DSpark draft model for speculative decoding. vLLM supports MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, on NVIDIA Rubin GPUs with dedicated Rubin kernels, and on AMD MI350-series GPUs, with strong performance on agentic workloads. Note that the model will only be available in the nightly PyPI wheel after the code is reviewed and merged upstream, which usually takes about a week. Full recipes are at vLLM Recipes , and the checkpoint is at MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.1-Flash . The MiniMax-M3 model family replaces full attention with a variant of block-sparse attention ( arXiv 2606.13392 ) to make inference more efficient. The KV cache is split into blocks of 128 tokens. A lightweight indexer scores every key in the context with one index query per GQA group against a single shared index-key head, then max-pools those scores into one score per block. Main attention then runs exactly, but only over the top 16 blocks, and the most recent block is always kept. That caps each query at 2,048 keys, however long the context is. The payoff is largest in decode, which is limited by memory bandwidth. Each step still scans the index keys for the whole context, but that is only 128 bytes per token per layer, an eighth of the 1,024 bytes of K/V that dense attention would read (FP8, 4 KV heads × 128 dims). The full K/V is then read for just the 2,048 selected tokens. At long-context decode, per-step HBM traffic drops to about 12.5% of what dense attention reads. Figure 1: MiniMax Sparse Attention. Each GQA group's indexer picks its top KV blocks, and every query head in that group attends exactly over only those blocks. Step through it. MiniMax-M3.1 greatly improves inference efficiency over the previous generation: it was natively quantization-aware trained for an NVFP4 KV cache, and its routed MoE weights are stored in NVFP4. The NVFP4 experts shrink the checkpoint from 451.5 GB (MiniMax-M3-MXFP8) to 250.1 GB, which is 44.6% smaller. The NVFP4 KV cache needs 34,560 bytes per token instead of 61,440 bytes in FP8, a saving of 43.75% per token. Together, on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs with DEP4 deployment and 256K-token sequences, M3.1 fits 76 concurrent sequences where M3 with an FP8 KV cache fits 28, about 2.7× as many on the same hardw

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the r
